=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. While prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 proportion (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this null result with a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in this regime.

=== introduction ===
Deep learning models deployed in edge AI environments frequently encounter distribution shifts that degrade performance, particularly in temporal domains where non-stationary dynamics are prevalent. The UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset exemplifies this challenge, requiring models to generalize across subjects whose movement patterns vary significantly despite belonging to the same activity classes. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay, mitigate overfitting but do not explicitly constrain the geometric structure of learned representations. Recent theoretical work suggests that the singular value spectrum of weight matrices influences generalization, yet the specific impact of spectral entropy on subject-disjoint robustness remains unexplored.

Current literature establishes that time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. While substantial progress has been made in algorithmic responses, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific weight geometries that facilitate robustness [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. However, length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding [11]. Furthermore, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, leaving open questions about how inductive biases impact performance [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, indicating that standard regularization strategies may be insufficient [17].

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training has been investigated for calibrated confidence under distribution shift, but results indicate it may actively impair performance in attention-based architectures [1]. Studies on latent variables suggest that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, complicating the hypothesis that spectral concentration aids robustness [5]. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that weight matrices exhibiting fast singular value decay allow for low-rank parameterization, yet this focuses on parameter efficiency rather than generalization margins [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve generalization by steering parameters away from sharp regions, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Additionally, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, necessitating richer algorithmic techniques [6].

Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections accelerates solving, suggesting that learned projections can capture structure [3]. Regularization by denoising utilizes denoising engines as regularization strategies for inverse problems through fixed-point projection [12]. However, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents significant challenges, highlighting the complexity of managing entropy in learned systems [13, 16]. Despite these advances, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers.

This paper addresses this gap by testing whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. We clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in generalization, guiding regularization design for resource-constrained edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical. Our contributions are:
- We preregister and execute a subject-disjoint evaluation of spectral entropy minimization on input projections using a Transformer architecture.
- We report null results across primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, indicating the intervention does not exceed the worthwhile margin.
- We provide negative controls to rule out confounding factors in the regularization implementation.

=== related_work ===
**Time Series and Out-of-Distribution Generalization**
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific weight geometries that facilitate robustness [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit task decomposition to learn efficiently, yet length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding [11]. Existing theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes [11]. Furthermore, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, leaving open questions about how inductive biases impact performance [7]. How to reduce the dependency on the number of labels and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, indicating that standard regularization strategies may be insufficient [17]. Regularization based approaches to continual learning cannot learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in elemental continual benchmarks, highlighting shortcomings in current strategies [17].

**Entropy and Weight Structure in Regularization**
Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training has been investigated for calibrated confidence, but findings indicate it does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Studies on latent variables suggest that the entropy of intermediate representations influences robustness to distributional shift, where removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance [5]. Conversely, top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution and out-of-distribution, suggesting a complex relationship between entropy and utility [5]. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing a low-rank parameterization [14]. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field independence assumptions [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Additionally, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, necessitating richer algorithmic techniques [6]. The practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization, yet no such technique has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these general settings [6].

**Projections and Regularization Mechanisms**
Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections accelerates solving, suggesting that learned projections can capture structure [3]. Learning projection matrices from data is beneficial, leading to significantly higher solution quality than existing random projection while greatly reducing solving time [3]. Regularization by denoising utilizes denoising engines as regularization strategies for inverse problems in image processing through fixed-point projection [12]. Reformulating regularization by denoising as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers provides guarantees for convergence [12]. Additionally, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents significant challenges, highlighting the complexity of managing entropy in learned systems [13]. Unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs in low-entropy scenarios [13]. Text watermarking presents significant challenges in low-entropy texts like code and mathematics, where tokens are hardly modifiable without changing intended meaning [16]. Existing research addresses this by relying on high-entropy tokens, yet detection accuracy remains suboptimal as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens [16]. These works collectively underscore the difficulty of manipulating entropy structures without compromising utility, a tension central to the present study.

=== method ===
The core intervention in this study is the enforcement of a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights via a regularization term added to the training objective. This operator targets the geometry of the weight matrix directly, hypothesizing that concentrating energy into dominant temporal modes facilitates feature learning in finite-width networks. The term computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the weight matrix, normalizes singular values to probabilities, and minimizes their entropy. This encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly. The hypothesis posits that this spectral concentration enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay.

The comparator condition employs standard weight decay without the spectral entropy term. This baseline neutralizes the effect of weight magnitude regularization, isolating the contribution of spectral structure. By holding weight decay constant across conditions, any observed difference in held-out classification accuracy can be attributed to the spectral entropy minimization rather than overall parameter norm constraints. The first negative control involves entropy minimization applied to a fixed noise parameter, ruling out effects driven by the optimization landscape of the entropy term itself rather than the weight structure. The second negative control involves fixed noise without entropy optimization, ensuring that stochasticity in the training process does not confound the results.

The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly manipulates the singular value distribution, which theoretical work suggests influences generalization bounds. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that weight matrices exhibiting fast singular value decay allow for low-rank parameterization, capturing structured weight correlations [14]. However, studies on latent variables suggest that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, creating a tension this experiment resolves empirically [5]. The comparator neutralizes magnitude effects, ensuring that the spectral shape, not the scale, is the variable of interest. This design aligns with findings that sharpness-aware minimization improves generalization by steering parameters away from sharp regions, suggesting that landscape geometry matters [2].

The implementation computes the SVD at each training step for the input projection layer. The singular values are normalized to sum to one, forming a probability distribution. The entropy of this distribution is calculated and added to the loss function with a weighting coefficient. This process encourages the singular values to converge to a sparse distribution, effectively reducing the rank of the effective transformation. The baseline condition omits this term, relying solely on weight decay to constrain the weights. The negative controls apply the entropy term to non-weight parameters or fix the noise, isolating the mechanism. This setup ensures that any performance difference is due to the spectral constraint on the input projections specifically.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. This dataset contains raw inertial signals organized into 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We use the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This split tests what this question asks because it ensures that the model must generalize to unseen subjects, simulating the distribution shift encountered in edge AI deployment. A random split would have hidden this challenge by allowing subject-specific features to leak into the training set, inflating accuracy estimates without proving robustness.

The model architecture is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions) and learned positional embedding (128 to 64 dimensions). It comprises 2 blocks, each with LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps, and feed-forward residuals. Training runs for 12 epochs with a batch size of 128 using SGD with learning rate 0.05 and momentum 0.9. The outcome definition is the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. This metric directly measures the practical utility of the model in the target domain.

We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Using this many seeds ensures that the results are not artifacts of specific initializations, providing statistical power to detect effects exceeding the worthwhile margin. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization variance, allowing paired statistical tests that are more sensitive to the intervention effect. The cost is increased computational budget, but this is necessary for a rigorous test of the hypothesis. The first negative control rules out optimization artifacts, and the second rules out stochasticity effects. Without these controls, it would be indistinguishable whether performance changes were due to the spectral constraint or the presence of any additional loss term. The analysis computes mean held-out classification accuracy with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for each condition.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan. Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9053 [0.902, 0.908], while the baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908]. The first negative control and the second negative control both achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908], performing comparably to the deterministic baseline.

Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the primary cohort. The learning curves for the proposed condition and the baseline overlap substantially throughout training, visually confirming the lack of divergence in performance. This suggests that the spectral entropy minimization did not alter the optimization trajectory in a way that benefited generalization. The negative controls also track the baseline closely, indicating that the additional loss term did not introduce instability.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Figure 3 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). Again, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.9087 [0.906, 0.912], while the baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91]. The negative controls both achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91].

Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the replication cohort. Similar to the primary cohort, the learning curves overlap, with the proposed condition showing no consistent advantage over the baseline. The replication cohort confirms the primary result, reinforcing the conclusion that the intervention does not yield a worthwhile improvement. The effect size in the replication cohort (Cohen's dz=0.25) is slightly larger than in the primary cohort (0.05), but the confidence interval still spans zero, preventing a claim of significance. The consistency across cohorts suggests the null result is robust to seed variation.

=== discussion ===
The results indicate that minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections does not enhance feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. This finding contradicts the hypothesis that spectral concentration facilitates generalization in this regime. While prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Our null result suggests that the mechanism proposed does not operate as anticipated in attention-based architectures.

This outcome aligns with findings that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Although our intervention minimized rather than maximized entropy, the lack of benefit suggests that explicit entropy manipulation of weight structures is not a reliable path to robustness in this context. Studies on latent variables suggest that low-entropy representations can hurt out-of-distribution performance, which may explain why constraining the spectral entropy did not help [5]. The removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance, implying that diversity in representations is valuable [5]. Our intervention reduced spectral diversity, potentially limiting the model's capacity to adapt to subject-specific variations.

Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that weight matrices exhibiting fast singular value decay allow for low-rank parameterization, capturing structured weight correlations [14]. However, our results suggest that enforcing this structure via regularization does not translate to improved generalization accuracy on subject-disjoint data. The parameter cost savings observed in Bayesian contexts may not apply to deterministic transformers trained with SGD. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Our spectral entropy term may not have effectively steered the model away from sharp regions, or the landscape geometry may not be the primary driver of generalization in this task.

The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the validity of the null result. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cases, as the confidence intervals included zero. This highlights the importance of replication in distinguishing true effects from noise. The negative controls performed comparably to the baseline, ruling out confounding factors related to the optimization of the entropy term itself. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in this regime. Future work should investigate whether spectral constraints are more effective in different architectures or domains, such as computer vision or language modeling, where weight structure may play a different role.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. The results may not generalize to other temporal domains or model families, such as recurrent neural networks or convolutional architectures. The spectral entropy minimization was applied only to the input projection weights; applying it to attention matrices or feed-forward layers might yield different results. The training budget was fixed at 12 epochs, and longer training schedules could potentially allow the regularization to take effect. The worthwhile margin was set at 0.0125098 proportion, which is stringent; smaller but practically relevant improvements might exist but remain undetected. Finally, the study focuses on subject-disjoint generalization, and the intervention might behave differently under other distribution shift scenarios, such as sensor drift or environmental changes.

=== conclusion ===
This study investigated whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks. The preregistered hypothesis predicted higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Results from both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts were inconclusive, with confidence intervals including zero. The proposed condition did not outperform the baseline or negative controls. These findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. For someone choosing between these methods, standard weight decay remains the preferable choice due to its simplicity and equivalent performance. Future work should explore alternative geometric constraints or focus on domains where spectral structure is more critically linked to generalization.

Related-work section:
**Time Series and Out-of-Distribution Generalization**
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific weight geometries that facilitate robustness [9]. Generalization bounds for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit task decomposition to learn efficiently, yet length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding [11]. Existing theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes [11]. Furthermore, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization in multi-label learning is still in the early stage, leaving open questions about how inductive biases impact performance [7]. How to reduce the dependency on the number of labels and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem [7]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, indicating that standard regularization strategies may be insufficient [17]. Regularization based approaches to continual learning cannot learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in elemental continual benchmarks, highlighting shortcomings in current strategies [17]. **Entropy and Weight Structure in Regularization**
Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift [1]. Entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training has been investigated for calibrated confidence, but findings indicate it does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Studies on latent variables suggest that the entropy of intermediate representations influences robustness to distributional shift, where removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance [5]. Conversely, top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution and out-of-distribution, suggesting a complex relationship between entropy and utility [5]. Singular Bayesian neural networks argue that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing a low-rank parameterization [14]. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field independence assumptions [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood [2]. Additionally, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, necessitating richer algorithmic techniques [6]. The practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization, yet no such technique has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these general settings [6]. **Projections and Regularization Mechanisms**
Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections accelerates solving, suggesting that learned projections can capture structure [3]. Learning projection matrices from data is beneficial, leading to significantly higher solution quality than existing random projection while greatly reducing solving time [3]. Regularization by denoising utilizes denoising engines as regularization strategies for inverse problems in image processing through fixed-point projection [12]. Reformulating regularization by denoising as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers provides guarantees for convergence [12]. Additionally, accurate detection of generated content in low-entropy scenarios presents significant challenges, highlighting the complexity of managing entropy in learned systems [13]. Unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs in low-entropy scenarios [13]. Text watermarking presents significant challenges in low-entropy texts like code and mathematics, where tokens are hardly modifiable without changing intended meaning [16]. Existing research addresses this by relying on high-entropy tokens, yet detection accuracy remains suboptimal as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens [16]. These works collectively underscore the difficulty of manipulating entropy structures without compromising utility, a tension central to the present study.

Cited papers and their abstracts:
[1] Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

[2] Generalization Aware Minimization
Abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms have effectively improved neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, which tend to generalize poorly. However, the underlying mechanisms of SAM are not fully understood, and recent studies question whether its bias toward flatter regions is why it improves generalization. In this work, we introduce Generalization-Aware Minimization (GAM), a generalized version of SAM that employs multiple perturbation steps instead of SAM's single-step perturbations. This allows GAM to directly guide model parameters toward areas of the landscape that generalize better. We show that the expected true (test) loss landscape is a rescaled version of the observed training loss landscape and demonstrate how GAM's multiple perturbative updates can be designed to optimize this expected true loss. Finally, we present a practical online algorithm that adapts GAM's perturbative steps during training to improve generalization, and we empirically validate its superior performance over SAM on benchmark datasets. We believe GAM sheds light on the generalization improvements of sharpness-based algorithms and can inspire the development of optimizers with even better generalization.

[3] Generalization Bound and Learning Methods for Data-Driven Projections in Linear Programming
Abstract: How to solve high-dimensional linear programs (LPs) efficiently is a fundamental question. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in reducing LP sizes using *random projections*, which can accelerate solving LPs independently of improving LP solvers. This paper explores a new direction of *data-driven projections*, which use projection matrices learned from data instead of random projection matrices. Given training data of $n$-dimensional LPs, we learn an $n\times k$ projection matrix with $n > k$. When addressing a future LP instance, we reduce its dimensionality from $n$ to $k$ via the learned projection matrix, solve the resulting LP to obtain a $k$-dimensional solution, and apply the learned matrix to it to recover an $n$-dimensional solution. On the theoretical side, a natural question is: how much data is sufficient to ensure the quality of recovered solutions? We address this question based on the framework of *data-driven algorithm design*, which connects the amount of data sufficient for establishing generalization bounds to the *pseudo-dimension* of performance metrics. We obtain an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(nk^2)$ upper bound on the pseudo-dimension, where $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}$ compresses logarithmic factors. We also provide an $\Omega(nk)$ lower bound, implying our result is tight up to an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(k)$ factor. On the practical side, we explore two simple methods for learning projection matrices: PCA- and gradient-based methods. While the former is relatively efficient, the latter can sometimes achieve better solution quality. Experiments demonstrate that learning projection matrices from data is indeed beneficial: it leads to significantly higher solution quality than the existing random projection while greatly reducing the time for solving LPs.

[4] Generalization Bound of Gradient Flow through Training Trajectory and Data-dependent Kernel
Abstract: Gradient-based optimization methods have shown remarkable empirical success, yet their theoretical generalization properties remain only partially understood. In this paper, we establish a generalization bound for gradient flow that aligns with the classical Rademacher complexity bounds for kernel methods—specifically those based on the RKHS norm and kernel trace—through a data-dependent kernel called the loss path kernel (LPK). Unlike static kernels such as NTK, the LPK captures the entire training trajectory, adapting to both data and optimization dynamics, leading to tighter and more informative generalization guarantees. Moreover, the bound highlights how the norm of the training loss gradients along the optimization trajectory influences the final generalization performance. The key technical ingredients in our proof combine stability analysis of gradient flow with uniform convergence via Rademacher complexity. Our bound recovers existing kernel regression bounds for overparameterized neural networks and shows the feature learning capability of neural networks compared to kernel methods. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets validate that our bounds correlate well with the true generalization gap.

[5] Low-Entropy Latent Variables Hurt Out-of-Distribution Performance
Abstract: We study the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift. We train models consisting of two feed-forward networks end-to-end separated by a discrete $n$-bit channel on an unsupervised contrastive learning task. Different masking strategies are applied after training that remove a proportion of low-entropy bits, high-entropy bits, or randomly selected bits, and the effects on performance are compared to the baseline accuracy with no mask. We hypothesize that the entropy of a bit serves as a guide to its usefulness out-of-distribution (OOD). Through experiment on three OOD datasets we demonstrate that the removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit OOD performance. Conversely, we find that top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution (InD) and OOD.

[6] Regularization and Optimal Multiclass Learning
Abstract: The quintessential learning algorithm of empirical risk minimization (ERM) is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning. Relatedly, the practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization. Nevertheless, no such technique or principle has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these more general settings. The purpose of this work is to precisely characterize the role of regularization in perhaps the simplest setting for which ERM fails: multiclass learning with arbitrary label sets. Using one-inclusion graphs (OIGs), we exhibit optimal learning algorithms that dovetail with tried-and-true algorithmic principles: Occam’s Razor as embodied by structural risk minimization (SRM), the principle of maximum entropy, and Bayesian inference. We also extract from OIGs a combinatorial sequence we term the Hall complexity, which is the first to characterize a problem’s transductive error rate exactly. Lastly, we introduce a generalization of OIGs and the transductive learning setting to the agnostic case, where we show that optimal orientations of Hamming graphs – judged using nodes’ outdegrees minus a system of node-dependent credits – characterize optimal learners exactly. We demonstrate that an agnostic version of the Hall complexity again characterizes error rates exactly, and exhibit an optimal learner using maximum entropy programs.

[7] Generalization Analysis for Multi-Label Learning
Abstract: Despite great advances in algorithms for multi-label learning, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization is still in the early stage. Some recent theoretical results has investigated the generalization performance of multi-label learning under several evaluation metrics, however, how to reduce the dependency on the number of labels, explicitly introduce label correlations, and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem. In an attempt to make up for the gap in the generalization theory of multi-label learning, we develop several novel vector-contraction inequalities, which exploit the Lipschitz continuity of loss functions, and derive generalization bounds with a weaker dependency on the number of labels than the state of the art in the case of decoupling the relationship among different components, which serves as theoretical guarantees for the generalization of multi-label learning. In addition, we derive the generalization bound for Macro-Averaged AUC and analyze its relationship with class-imbalance. The mild bounds without strong assumptions explain the good generalization ability of multi-label learning with first-order label correlations and high-order label correlations induced by norm regularizers.

[8] Minimization of the Training Makespan in Hybrid Federated Split Learning
Abstract: Parallel Split Learning (SL) allows resource-constrained devices that cannot participate in Federated Learning (FL) to train deep neural networks (NNs) by splitting the NN model into parts. In particular, such devices (clients) may offload the processing task of the largest model part to a computationally powerful helper, and multiple helpers may be employed and work in parallel. In hybrid federated and split learning (HFSL), on the other hand, devices can participate in the training process through any of the two protocols (SL and FL), depending on the system's characteristics. This could considerably reduce the maximum training time over all clients (makespan), especially in highly heterogeneous scenarios. In this paper, we study the joint problem of the training protocol selection, client-helper assignments, and scheduling decisions, to minimize the training makespan. We prove this problem is NP-hard and propose two solution methods: one based on the decomposition of the problem by leveraging its inherent symmetry, and a second fully scalable one. Through numerical evaluations using our testbed's measurements, we build a solution strategy comprising these methods. Moreover, this strategy finds a near-optimal solution and achieves a shorter makespan than the baseline schemes by up to 71%.

[9] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[10] Generalization Bounds for Autoregressive Processes and In-Context Learning
Abstract: In this paper, we derive generalization results for next-token risk minimization in autoregressive processes of unbounded order. Our starting point is to relate the empirical loss to the denoising loss, which requires no additional assumptions compared to fixed-order Markovian models. We then show that, under a mixing or rephrasability condition on the data-generating process and ass[redacted]g a stable hypothesis class, the out-of-sample generalization error concentrates around the denoising error. These results characterize sample complexity in terms of the number of tokens, rather than the number of i.i.d. sequences. As a primary application, we interpret in-context learning as a special case of autoregressive prediction and derive sample complexity bounds under similar conditions. Importantly, the properties of individual in-context tasks determine the generalization rates, without requiring assumptions on mixture processes. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit the task decomposition to learn efficiently.

[11] Length Generalization via Auxiliary Tasks
Abstract: _Length generalization_, the ability of sequence models to generalize to sequences longer than those encountered during training, remains a key challenge for transformers, especially in tasks requiring algorithmic reasoning. Existing theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes or architectural variants, while empirical approaches frequently rely on ad hoc and often fragile techniques. In this work we introduce a novel framework for analyzing and proving length generalization bounds under specified, verifiable assumptions. A key outcome of the theory is the identification of a natural set of _auxiliary_ tasks, intricately related to the primary task structure, such that strong performance on these auxiliary tasks, alongside the primary task, provably guarantees length generalization within the framework. This motivates a multi-task training procedure that explicitly optimizes performance on both the primary and the identified auxiliary tasks. Empirical evaluations on a variety of synthetic benchmarks known to be challenging for length generalization, including sequence sorting, and reversal, demonstrate that our proposed method yields significant improvements in generalization to substantially longer sequences.

[12] Regularization by Denoising via Fixed-Point Projection (RED-PRO)
Abstract: Inverse problems in image processing are typically cast as optimization tasks, consisting of data-fidelity and stabilizing regularization terms. A recent regularization strategy of great interest utilizes the power of denoising engines. Two such methods are the Plug-and-Play Prior (PnP) and Regularization by Denoising (RED). While both have shown state-of-the-art results in various recovery tasks, their theoretical justification is incomplete. In this paper, we aim to bridge between RED and PnP, enriching the understanding of both frameworks. Towards that end, we reformulate RED as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection (RED-PRO) onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers. We offer a simple iterative solution to this problem, by which we show that PnP proximal gradient method is a special case of RED-PRO, while providing guarantees for the convergence of both frameworks to globally optimal solutions. In addition, we present relaxations of RED-PRO that allow for handling denoisers with limited fixed-point sets. Finally, we demonstrate RED-PRO for the tasks of image deblurring and super-resolution, showing improved results with respect to the original RED framework.

[13] A Watermark for Low-entropy and Unbiased Generation in Large Language Models
Abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have highlighted the risk of misusing them, raising the need for accurate detection of LLM-generated content. In response, a viable solution is to inject imperceptible identifiers into LLMs, known as watermarks. Previous work demonstrates that unbiased watermarks ensure unforgeability and preserve text quality by maintaining the expectation of the LLM output probability distribution. However, previous unbiased watermarking methods suffer from one or more of the following issues: (1) requiring access to white-box LLMs during detection, (2) incurring long detection time, (3) being not robust against simple watermarking attacks, (4) failing to provide statistical guarantees for the type II error of watermark detection, and (5) being not statistically unbiased for low-entropy scenarios, which hinder their deployment in practice. This study proposes the Sampling One Then Accepting (STA-1) method, a watermark that can address all of these issues. Moreover, we discuss the tradeoff between watermark strength and text quality for unbiased watermarks. We show that in low-entropy scenarios, unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Experimental results on both low-entropy and high-entropy datasets demonstrate that STA-1 achieves text quality and watermark strength comparable to existing unbiased watermarks, with a low risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Implementation codes for this study are available online (hidden for peer review).

[14] Singular Bayesian Neural Networks
Abstract: Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay. By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is \emph{singular} with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field's independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.

[15] Minimization I.I.D. Prophet Inequality via Extreme Value Theory: A Unified Approach
Abstract: The I.I.D. Prophet Inequality is a fundamental problem where, given $n$ independent random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ drawn from a known distribution $\mathcal{D}$, one has to decide at every step $i$ whether to stop and accept $X_i$ or discard it forever and continue. The goal is to maximize or minimize the selected value and compete against the all-knowing prophet. For maximization, a tight constant-competitive guarantee of $\approx 0.745$ is well-known (Correa et al, 2019), whereas minimization is qualitatively different: the optimal constant is distribution-dependent and can be arbitrarily large (Livanos and Mehta, 2024). In this paper, we provide a novel framework via the lens of Extreme Value Theory to analyze optimal threshold algorithms. We show that the competitive ratio for the minimization setting has a closed form described by a function $\Lambda$, which depends only on the extreme value index $\gamma$; in particular, it corresponds to $\Lambda(\gamma)$ for $\gamma \leq 0$. Despite the contrast of maximization and minimization, our framework turns out to be universal and we recover the results of (Kennedy and Kertz, 1991) for maximization as well. Surprisingly, the optimal competitive ratio for maximization is given by the same function $\Lambda(\gamma)$, but for $\gamma \geq 0$. Along the way, we obtain several results on the algorithm and the prophet's objectives from the perspective of extreme value theory, which might be of independent interest. We next study single-threshold algorithms for minimization. Using extreme value theory, we generalize the results of (Livanos and Mehta, 2024) which hold only for special classes of distributions, and obtain poly-logarithmic in $n$ guarantees. Finally, we consider the $k$-multi-unit prophet inequality for minimization and show that there exist constant-competitive single-threshold algorithms when $k \geq \log{n}$.

[16] Low-Entropy Watermark Detection via Bayes' Rule Derived Detector
Abstract: Text watermarking, which modify tokens to embed watermark, has proven effective in detecting machine-generated texts. Yet its application to low-entropy texts like code and mathematics presents significant challenges. A fair number of tokens in these texts are hardly modifiable without changing the intended meaning, causing statistical measures to falsely indicate the absence of a watermark. Existing research addresses this issue by rely mainly on a limited number of high-entropy tokens, which are considered flexible for modification, and accurately reflecting watermarks. However, their detection accuracy remains suboptimal, as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens modified through watermarking. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Bayes’ Rule derived Watermark Detector (BRWD), which exploit watermark information from every token, by leveraging the posterior probability of watermark’s presence. We theoretically prove the optimality of our method in terms of detection accuracy, and demonstrate its superiority across various datasets, models, and watermark injection strategies. Notably, our method achieves up to 50% and 70% relative improvements in detection accuracy over the best baselines in code generation and math problem-solving tasks, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/cczslp/BRWD.

[17] Regularization Shortcomings for Continual Learning
Abstract: In most machine learning algorithms, training data is assumed to be independent and identically distributed (iid). When it is not the case, the algorithm's performances are challenged, leading to the famous phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting. Algorithms dealing with it are gathered in the Continual Learning research field. In this paper, we study the regularization based approaches to continual learning and show that those approaches can not learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in an elemental continual benchmark: the class-incremental scenario. We make theoretical reasoning to prove this shortcoming and illustrate it with examples and experiments. Moreover, we show that it can have some important consequences on continual multi-tasks reinforcement learning or in pre-trained models used for continual learning. We believe that highlighting and understanding the shortcomings of regularization strategies will help us to use them more efficiently.

RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.

=== abstract ===
Regularization design for resource-constrained edge AI requires clarity on how weight spectra influence generalization under distribution shift. This Registered Report investigates whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 proportion (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline, failing to exceed the margin. The replication cohort confirmed this null result with a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). Negative controls performed comparably to the baseline. These findings indicate that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in time-series transformers.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification in edge AI settings demands models that generalize robustly across subjects, yet distribution shifts between training and deployment populations frequently degrade performance. Standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under such shifts, prompting investigation into regularization strategies that constrain weight geometry to improve out-of-distribution generalization. While substantial progress has been made in understanding distribution shifts in time series, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking regarding the specific mechanisms that facilitate robustness in finite-width networks [9]. Current literature identifies that time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization, yet the role of weight spectra in this context remains underexplored.

Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness, but findings are mixed regarding whether constraining or expanding entropy aids generalization. Some studies investigate whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift, while others argue that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay. Despite these advances, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This gap leaves practitioners without evidence on whether spectral constraints on input layers offer advantages over standard weight decay for temporal feature learning.

This paper addresses this open problem through a preregistered Registered Report. We test whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. The study operates in the regime where approximations needed to make Bayesian formalisms tractable are where the guarantees are lost, precisely the setting where explicit spectral regularization might offer value. We utilize a subject-disjoint split to ensure evaluation reflects true distribution shift rather than random variation within subjects.

The contributions of this work are:
- We provide a preregistered test of spectral entropy minimization on input projections for subject-disjoint time-series classification.
- We report null results across primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, indicating no accuracy benefit over standard weight decay.
- We clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in generalization, guiding regularization design for resource-constrained edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical.

=== related_work ===
**Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series**
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Generalization results for autoregressive processes relate empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. However, length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding, particularly in tasks requiring algorithmic reasoning [11]. When training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, observing that regularization based approaches can not learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in elemental continual benchmarks [17]. Collectively, this literature establishes that distribution shift is a fundamental barrier in temporal learning, yet specific weight geometries that mitigate this shift remain undefined.

**Entropy and Weight Structure in Regularization**
Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness, though consensus on the direction of entropy manipulation is absent. One study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift, finding that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. Conversely, other work studies the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift, demonstrating that the removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit out-of-distribution performance [5]. Regarding weight matrices specifically, arguments exist that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing low-rank parameterization to capture structured weight correlations [14]. Additionally, Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, suggesting landscape geometry matters more than explicit entropy constraints [2]. The tension between these findings suggests that while weight structure matters, the optimal entropy regime for input projections is unsettled.

**Projections and Dimensionality**
Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization, though primarily in non-temporal domains. Work explores reducing linear program sizes using random and data-driven projections to accelerate solving, demonstrating that learning projection matrices from data leads to significantly higher solution quality than existing random projection [3]. In image processing, regularization strategies utilize denoising engines for inverse problems through fixed-point projection, bridging frameworks to provide guarantees for convergence to globally optimal solutions [12]. However, neither line of work addresses spectral entropy minimization on input projections for temporal transformers under subject-disjoint shift. This study positions itself against these methods by testing whether spectral constraints on the input layer specifically aid temporal feature learning where projection methods have otherwise shown promise in static domains.

=== method ===
The core intervention enforces a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights via a regularization term added to the training objective. This operator computes the singular value decomposition of the weight matrix, normalizes singular values to probabilities, and minimizes their entropy. This encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly across all singular directions. The hypothesis posits that concentrating spectral energy improves feature learning for hard temporal tasks by reducing noise in the input representation.

The comparator is standard weight decay without the spectral entropy term. This baseline neutralizes the effect of regularization magnitude, isolating the spectral entropy constraint as the variable of interest. Standard weight decay is the prevailing practice for resource-constrained edge AI, making it the appropriate reference point for assessing practical utility. The first negative control involves entropy maximization to test whether the direction of the entropy constraint matters, while the second negative control involves fixed noise to rule out optimization artifacts.

The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly targets the singular value distribution of the input projection, which governs how temporal signals are mapped into the model's latent space. If low-entropy spectra facilitate robustness, this term should enhance held-out classification accuracy. The comparator neutralizes general regularization effects, ensuring any observed difference stems from the spectral constraint rather than weight magnitude suppression. The negative controls rule out confounds where any entropy term might alter optimization dynamics irrespective of direction.

This design tests the specific weight geometry that facilitates feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks. By focusing on the input projection, we isolate the feature extraction stage from deeper attention mechanisms. The method does not alter the attention blocks or positional embeddings, ensuring the intervention targets only the initial temporal mapping. This specificity allows us to attribute outcomes directly to the input weight spectrum rather than downstream capacity changes.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design employs a subject-disjoint split to test generalization under distribution shift, which a random split would have hidden. Subject-disjoint evaluation ensures that training and testing data come from distinct individuals, simulating the deployment scenario where models encounter unseen users. This split tests what this question asks because robustness to subject variation is critical for edge AI applications in human activity recognition. A random split would inflate accuracy by allowing leakage of subject-specific features, masking the true generalization gap.

Pairing every condition on one seed buys comparability across conditions while costing independence between arms. By using the same random seed for initialization and data ordering across the proposed condition, baseline, and negative controls, we reduce variance in the paired contrast estimate. This pairing allows us to detect smaller effect sizes with fewer seeds, though it requires careful interpretation to ensure seed-specific artifacts do not drive results. We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds to ensure sufficient power to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin. This number of seeds balances computational cost with the precision needed to resolve small accuracy differences in classification tasks.

The first negative control rules out the possibility that any entropy term improves performance regardless of direction, while the second negative control rules out optimization artifacts from the singular value decomposition computation. Without these controls, an improvement in the proposed condition could be indistinguishable from general regularization effects or numerical instability. The analysis uses paired randomisation tests to account for the seed pairing, reporting Cohen's dz to quantify effect size independent of sample size. The confirmatory-replication cohort uses disjoint seeds to verify that primary results are not seed-specific. This design ensures that null results are robust across independent random initializations.

=== results ===
We report results for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan. Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). The 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive as the lower bound did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The baseline achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908], while the proposed condition achieved 0.9053 [0.902, 0.908]. The first negative control and second negative control both achieved 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908], matching the baseline.

Figure 2 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the primary cohort. Learning curves overlap substantially, with no divergence suggesting latent benefits during training. The proposed condition tracks the baseline closely throughout the 12 epochs, reinforcing the final metric null result.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, Figure 3 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). Again, no statistically significant difference was observed as the 95% confidence interval includes zero. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. The baseline achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91], while the proposed condition achieved 0.9087 [0.906, 0.912]. The negative controls both achieved 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91], consistent with the baseline.

Figure 4 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the replication cohort. Similar to the primary cohort, learning curves remain overlapping. The proposed condition shows a slight numerical uplift in final accuracy but fails to separate from the baseline confidence interval. The replication cohort confirms the primary finding that spectral entropy minimization does not yield a reliable accuracy benefit exceeding the worthwhile margin. Both cohorts indicate that the intervention is indistinguishable from standard weight decay in this setting.

=== discussion ===
The quantitative findings refute the hypothesis that minimizing spectral entropy of input projections enhances subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. In both primary and replication cohorts, the proposed condition failed to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin, with confidence intervals encompassing zero. This null result aligns with prior work indicating that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance [1]. While that study tested entropy maximization, the failure of entropy minimization here suggests that explicit entropy constraints on weights may not be the lever for robustness in this regime.

The results contradict the implication that singular value decay inherently aids generalization accuracy, though they do not contradict findings that such decay reduces parameter cost. Prior work argues that the parameter cost of standard Bayesian neural networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing low-rank parameterization to capture structured weight correlations [14]. Our findings suggest that while low-rank structures may save parameters, enforcing low spectral entropy on full-rank input projections does not improve accuracy. This distinguishes parameter efficiency from generalization performance, clarifying that weight geometry benefits may be limited to compression rather than robustness.

Regarding the broader literature on out-of-distribution generalization in time series, the null result underscores the difficulty of improving upon standard regularization. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization, yet simple spectral constraints do not resolve these challenges [9]. The finding that negative controls performed comparably to the baseline further indicates that the optimization dynamics introduced by the spectral term do not inadvertently aid training. This extends the understanding of regularization shortcomings for continual learning, observing that when training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, and additional regularizers may not suffice [17].

For practitioners choosing between these methods, the results recommend standard weight decay over spectral entropy minimization. The intervention adds computational overhead from singular value decomposition without accuracy gains. This guidance is critical for resource-constrained edge AI where subject-disjoint robustness is critical, as unnecessary complexity should be avoided. The results confirm that standard regularization remains the robust choice for temporal feature learning in this architecture. Future work should investigate whether spectral constraints aid deeper layers or different architectures, as the input projection may not be the sensitive locus for spectral regularization.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. Results may not generalize to other temporal domains such as speech or financial series where signal characteristics differ. The spectral entropy term was applied only to the input projection weights; deeper layers may respond differently to spectral constraints. The worthwhile margin was fixed preregistered, and while the study was powered to detect it, smaller but practically relevant effects below this threshold cannot be ruled out. The subject-disjoint split tests one form of distribution shift, but other shifts such as sensor drift or activity definition changes remain untested. Finally, the computational cost of singular value decomposition was not measured in wall-clock time, though it is theoretically higher than standard weight decay.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report tested whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported in either primary or replication cohorts, with accuracy differences failing to exceed the worthwhile margin. The proposed condition performed comparably to standard weight decay and negative controls. These findings indicate that spectral entropy minimization does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in this regime. Future work should explore spectral constraints in deeper layers or alternative architectures to determine if weight geometry plays a role elsewhere in the network.

=== references ===
[1] ABS AI RSE. Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness (n.d.).
[2] Akhilan Boopathy, Ila R Fiete. Generalization Aware Minimization (2024).
[3] Shinsaku Sakaue, Taihei Oki. Generalization Bound and Learning Methods for Data-Driven Projections in Linear Programming (2024).
[5] Nandi Schoots, Dylan Cope. Low-Entropy Latent Variables Hurt Out-of-Distribution Performance (2023).
[6] Julian Asilis, Siddartha Devic et al. Regularization and Optimal Multiclass Learning (2024).
[7] Yifan Zhang, Min-Ling Zhang. Generalization Analysis for Multi-Label Learning (2024).
[9] Xin Wu, Fei Teng et al. Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey (2025).
[10] Oğuz Kaan Yüksel, Nicolas Flammarion. Generalization Bounds for Autoregressive Processes and In-Context Learning (2025).
[11] Pranjal Awasthi, Anupam Gupta et al. Length Generalization via Auxiliary Tasks (2025).
[12] Regev Cohen, Michael Elad et al. Regularization by Denoising via Fixed-Point Projection (RED-PRO) (2025).
[13] Minjia Mao, Dongjun Wei et al. A Watermark for Low-entropy and Unbiased Generation in Large Language Models (2024).
[14] Mame Diarra Toure, David A. Stephens. Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (2026).
[16] Beining Huang, Du Su et al. Low-Entropy Watermark Detection via Bayes' Rule Derived Detector (2025).
[17] Timothée Lesort, Andrei Stoian et al. Regularization Shortcomings for Continual Learning (2019).
